### Big hidden bug candidates: In `03_migracion_fnbc.sql`, trigger detects DF1 but has a serious flaw: It is created **after** the view and tables; but the view `v_control_lote_almacen` is not a table, so the trigger's `SELECT ... FROM v_control_lote_almacen GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` under *statement-level* trigger after an INSERT works. However when the trigger itself is created on `control_lote`, any INSERT into `control_lote` fires. When `fn_control_lote_df1` runs, it queries the view, which includes the new rows. Good.

But **the trigger on `responsable_deposito` AFTER UPDATE OF deposito_id** checks view after update. Suppose a responsable with multiple lotes is moved to a new depot where another responsable of that depot controls some of same lotes. The view will show >1 for (lote,deposito) → raises. Good.

But there is a **critical missing check**: The migration function's exception message uses `v_lote, v_dep` variables selected; `IF FOUND` after `SELECT ... INTO` is true only if a row found; `FOUND` in PL/pgSQL is set by SELECT INTO. fine.

### Analyze `03_migracion` data preservation more thoroughly:

Original `control_lote_almacen` has PK (lote,deposito) and DF2 R->D. Decomposition:
R1=responsable_deposito(R,D) with R PK. Insert DISTINCT R,D. Since DF2 holds, each R has one D → count = distinct R. R2=control_lote(L,R) PK. Insert L,R from original. Since original PK (L,D) and each R->D, if two rows with same L and same R but different D impossible (R->D), so (L,R) unique. Good. View join gives original rows. fine.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Recrea la base $DB (por defecto tpi_food_store), corre todos los scripts en orden y guarda la salida en evidencias/.
set -u
DB="${DB:-tpi_food_store}"
export PGUSER="${PGUSER:-postgres}"
cd "$(dirname "$0")"
mkdir -p evidencias

echo ">> Recreando la base $DB"
dropdb --if-exists "$DB" && createdb "$DB" || exit 1

# Construcci��n: sin errores y en una sola transacci��n. Cada evidencia muestra quǸ ejecut�� y quǸ qued�� creado.
declare -A verificar=(
  [01_schema]="SELECT table_name AS tabla, COUNT(*) AS columnas FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema = 'public' GROUP BY table_name ORDER BY table_name;"
  [02_data]="SELECT 'categoria' AS tabla, COUNT(*) AS filas FROM categoria UNION ALL SELECT 'producto', COUNT(*) FROM producto UNION ALL SELECT 'cliente', COUNT(*) FROM cliente UNION ALL SELECT 'pedido', COUNT(*) FROM pedido UNION ALL SELECT 'detalle_pedido', COUNT(*) FROM detalle_pedido UNION ALL SELECT 'usuario', COUNT(*) FROM usuario;"
  [02b_carga_masiva_rapida]="SELECT 'producto' AS tabla, COUNT(*) AS filas FROM producto UNION ALL SELECT 'cliente', COUNT(*) FROM cliente UNION ALL SELECT 'pedido', COUNT(*) FROM pedido UNION ALL SELECT 'detalle_pedido', COUNT(*) FROM detalle_pedido;"
  [03_restricciones]="SELECT event_object_table AS tabla, trigger_name AS trigger, action_timing AS momento, string_agg(event_manipulation, ', ') AS eventos FROM information_schema.triggers WHERE trigger_schema = 'public' GROUP BY 1, 2, 3 ORDER BY 1, 2;"
  [04_indices]="SELECT tablename AS tabla, indexname AS indice, indexdef AS definicion FROM pg_indexes WHERE schemaname = 'public' ORDER BY 1, 2;"
  [05_vistas]="SELECT table_name AS vista FROM information_schema.views WHERE table_schema = 'public' ORDER BY 1;"
  [05b_materializadas]="SELECT matviewname AS vista_materializada, ispopulated AS con_datos, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM mv_facturacion_cat_mes) AS filas FROM pg_matviews;"
  [06_funciones_procedimientos]="SELECT routine_name AS nombre, routine_type AS tipo, external_language AS lenguaje FROM information_schema.routines WHERE routine_schema = 'public' AND routine_name IN ('fn_total_pedido', 'sp_registrar_pedido') ORDER BY 1;"
)
estrictos=(01_schema 02_data 02b_carga_masiva_rapida 03_restricciones 04_indices 05_vistas 05b_materializadas 06_funciones_procedimientos)
for s in "${estrictos[@]}"; do
  echo ">> $s"
  out="evidencias/$s.txt"
  echo "===== Ejecuci��n de sql/$s.sql =====" > "$out"
  PGOPTIONS="-c client_min_messages=warning" psql -d "$DB" -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 --single-transaction -f "sql/$s.sql" >> "$out" 2>&1 \
       || { echo "   ERROR en $s (ver $out)"; exit 1; }
  { echo; echo "===== Verificaci��n: quǸ qued�� creado ====="; psql -d "$DB" -c "${verificar[$s]}"; } >> "$out" 2>&1
done

# Pruebas: incluyen errores esperados, se muestran con eco (-a).
pruebas=(02c_verificacion_carga_masiva 03b_pruebas_restricciones 07_consultas 08_transacciones 09_soft_delete 10_auditoria_precios 11_optimizacion)
for s in "${pruebas[@]}"; do
  echo ">> $s"
  psql -d "$DB" -a -f "sql/$s.sql" > "evidencias/$s.txt" 2>&1
done

# Concurrencia: dos sesiones reales. La sesi��n B arranca 1 s despuǸs que la A.
dos_sesiones() {  # $1 = archivo de salida, $2 = t��tulo, $3 = comandos de A (separados por |pausa|), $4 = comandos de B
  local out="evidencias/$1.txt" a1="${3%%|pausa|*}" a2="${3#*|pausa|}"
  { echo "$a1"; sleep 2; echo "$a2"; } | psql -d "$DB" -a > /tmp/sesion_a.txt 2>&1 &
  sleep 1
  echo "$4" | psql -d "$DB" -a > /tmp/sesion_b.txt 2>&1
  wait
  { echo "===== $2 ====="; echo; echo "----- SESI�"N A -----"; cat /tmp/sesion_a.txt
    echo; echo "----- SESI�"N B (arranca 1 s despuǸs) -----"; cat /tmp/sesion_b.txt; } > "$out"
}
echo ">> 08b / 08c / 08d (dos sesiones)"
CONTAR="SELECT COUNT(*) AS pedidos_cliente_10 FROM pedido WHERE id_cliente = 10;"
INSERTAR="INSERT INTO pedido (forma_pago, id_cliente) VALUES ('EFECTIVO', 10);"

  "BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED; $CONTAR|pausa|$CONTAR COMMIT;" "$INSERTAR"

  "BEGIN;
SELECT id_producto, stock FROM producto WHERE id_producto = 20 FOR UPDATE;
SELECT clock_timestamp() - now() AS tiempo_de_espera;
COMMIT;"

echo ">> Listo. Revisǭ la carpeta evidencias/."

-- 03 �?" Reglas de negocio con triggers

-- REGLA 1 �?" Producto inactivo

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION fn_verificar_producto_activo()
RETURNS TRIGGER AS $$
DECLARE
    v_activo BOOLEAN;
BEGIN
    SELECT activo INTO v_activo
      FROM producto
     WHERE id_producto = NEW.id_producto;

    IF v_activo = FALSE THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION 'No se puede vender el producto con id %: estǭ dado de baja (activo = FALSE)',
                        NEW.id_producto;
    END IF;

    RETURN NEW;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS trg_verificar_producto_activo ON detalle_pedido;

CREATE TRIGGER trg_verificar_producto_activo
    BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE
    ON detalle_pedido
    FOR EACH ROW
    EXECUTE FUNCTION fn_verificar_producto_activo();

-- REGLA 2 �?" Stock insuficiente

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION fn_verificar_stock_suficiente()
RETURNS TRIGGER AS $$
DECLARE
    v_stock INTEGER;
BEGIN
    SELECT stock INTO v_stock
      FROM producto
     WHERE id_producto = NEW.id_producto;

    IF NEW.cantidad > v_stock THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION 'Stock insuficiente para el producto con id %: se solicitan % unidades, pero hay % en stock',
                        NEW.id_producto, NEW.cantidad, v_stock;
    END IF;

    RETURN NEW;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS trg_verificar_stock_suficiente ON detalle_pedido;

CREATE TRIGGER trg_verificar_stock_suficiente
    BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE
    ON detalle_pedido
    FOR EACH ROW
    EXECUTE FUNCTION fn_verificar_stock_suficiente();

```

-- 05b �?" Vista materializada: facturaci��n por categor��a y mes

DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW IF EXISTS mv_facturacion_cat_mes CASCADE;

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_facturacion_cat_mes AS
SELECT
    c.id_categoria,
    c.nombre AS categoria,
    DATE_TRUNC('month', pe.fecha) AS mes,
    COUNT(DISTINCT pe.id_pedido) AS cantidad_pedidos,
    SUM(dp.cantidad * dp.precio_unitario) AS facturacion_total
FROM categoria c
JOIN producto p       ON p.id_categoria = c.id_categoria
JOIN detalle_pedido dp ON dp.id_producto = p.id_producto
JOIN pedido pe        ON pe.id_pedido = dp.id_pedido
WHERE c.activo = TRUE AND p.activo = TRUE
GROUP BY c.id_categoria, c.nombre, DATE_TRUNC('month', pe.fecha);

-- �?ndice ǧnico: requisito para REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_mv_facturacion_cat_mes
    ON mv_facturacion_cat_mes (id_categoria, mes);

### **Potential bug**: `verificacion_permisos.sql` line 166-173 `admin_datos` updates `producto` price and expects `auditoria_precio` trigger to record. The trigger `fn_auditar_precios` is SECURITY DEFINER (U5 01) and uses `current_user` in `auditoria_precio` default: `usuario_bd TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT current_user`. In a SECURITY DEFINER trigger, `current_user` is the function owner (postgres), not admin_datos. So the audit will record `postgres`, losing accountability. Wait: `fn_auditar_precios` was altered to SECURITY DEFINER in U5 01. `auditoria_precio.usuario_bd DEFAULT current_user` is evaluated in the INSERT inside the function, where `current_user` is the function owner (`postgres`) because SECURITY DEFINER. The original trigger before U5 ran as invoker, recording admin_datos. After U5, it records postgres. This is a **security/audit bug**: the audit trail no longer records the actual database user. The `auditoria_seguridad` table uses `rol_bd TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT session_user`, specifically to avoid this; but `auditoria_precio` uses `current_user`. This is a strong finding!

Let's verify: `auditoria_precio` created in `sql/10_auditoria_precios.sql`:
```
usuario_bd TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT current_user,
```
Trigger function `fn_auditar_precios` inserts only `detalle`, so default `current_user` applies. U5 `01_auth_funciones.sql` line 96 `ALTER FUNCTION fn_auditar_precios() SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path...`. Then when admin_datos updates price, trigger runs as postgres; `current_user` = postgres; audit row `usuario_bd='postgres'`. So accountability lost. This is exactly the kind of subtle bug. Verification in DB: 
```
BEGIN;
SET ROLE admin_datos;
UPDATE producto SET precio=precio+1 WHERE id_producto=1;
RESET ROLE;
SELECT usuario_bd, detalle FROM auditoria_precio ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1;
ROLLBACK;
```
Should show postgres, not admin_datos. Or `SELECT current_user, session_user` inside. Great finding.

  - `trabajos-practicos/unidad5_seguridad/sql/01_auth_funciones.sql`: `ALTER FUNCTION fn_auditar_precios() SECURITY DEFINER` hace que `auditoria_precio.usuario_bd DEFAULT current_user` registre `postgres` en vez del usuario real (`admin_datos`), perdiendo trazabilidad.   - `trabajos-practicos/unidad5_seguridad/scripts/simulacro_incidente.sh`: los controles de contraseñas/mails solo imprimen conteo con `|| true`; no fallan el script si hay fuga.

1: -- U5 · roles.sql — Roles y permisos de Food Store con mínimo privilegio
2: --
3: -- Se ejecuta como postgres sobre la base del proyecto y se puede repetir: los roles se
4: -- crean si no existen y, antes de otorgar, se revoca todo lo anterior. Así, el resultado
5: -- es siempre exactamente lo que dice este archivo.
6: --
7: -- Las contraseñas NO se escriben acá. Después de correrlo, en psql:
8: --   \password app_web       \password admin_datos
9: --   \password usr_soporte   \password usr_reportes   \password usr_auditor
10: --
11: -- Justificación de cada rol (una oración cada uno):
12: --   rol_app_lectura   La tienda web muestra el catálogo y los pedidos: lee categorías, productos y pedidos, y nada con datos personales.
13: --   rol_app_escritura La tienda web registra ventas: inserta pedidos y sus líneas y descuenta stock, sin poder cambiar precios.
14: --   rol_soporte       La mesa de ayuda atiende a usuarios y clientes: los consulta sin ver contraseñas, corrige el celular o la baja, y resetea contraseñas solo con la función.
15: --   rol_reportes      El área comercial mira resultados agregados: lee vistas de ventas y la tabla anonimizada de usuarios, nunca datos personales.
16: --   rol_auditor       (adicional) Quien investiga un incidente lee los registros de auditoría, y ningún dato del negocio.
17: --   app_web           Login de la aplicación: lectura + escritura de la tienda y la función de autenticación.
18: --   admin_datos       Login del administrador de datos: todo sobre las tablas del esquema salvo modificar la auditoría, sin ser superusuario ni poder crear roles.
19: --   usr_soporte, usr_reportes, usr_auditor  (adicionales) Logins personales de cada área, para que el log diga quién hizo qué.
20: 
21: \set ON_ERROR_STOP on
22: 
23: -- 1. Crear los roles si no existen ------------------------------------------------
24: DO $$
25: DECLARE
26:     r TEXT;
27: BEGIN
28:     FOREACH r IN ARRAY ARRAY['rol_app_lectura', 'rol_app_escritura', 'rol_soporte', 'rol_reportes', 'rol_auditor'] LOOP
29:         IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname = r) THEN
30:             EXECUTE format('CREATE ROLE %I NOLOGIN', r);
31:         END IF;
32:     END LOOP;
33:     FOREACH r IN ARRAY ARRAY['app_web', 'admin_datos', 'usr_soporte', 'usr_reportes', 'usr_auditor'] LOOP
34:         IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname = r) THEN
35:             EXECUTE format('CREATE ROLE %I LOGIN', r);
36:         END IF;
37:     END LOOP;
38: END $$;
39: 
40: -- Ningún rol es superusuario ni puede crear roles o bases.
41: ALTER ROLE app_web      NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE NOBYPASSRLS CONNECTION LIMIT 20;
42: ALTER ROLE admin_datos  NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE NOBYPASSRLS CONNECTION LIMIT 3;
43: ALTER ROLE usr_soporte  NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE NOBYPASSRLS CONNECTION LIMIT 5;
44: ALTER ROLE usr_reportes NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE NOBYPASSRLS CONNECTION LIMIT 5;
45: ALTER ROLE usr_auditor  NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE NOBYPASSRLS CONNECTION LIMIT 2;
46: 
47: -- 2. Punto de partida limpio -------------------------------------------------------
48: DO $$
49: DECLARE
50:     r TEXT;
51: BEGIN
52:     FOREACH r IN ARRAY ARRAY['rol_app_lectura', 'rol_app_escritura', 'rol_soporte', 'rol_reportes', 'rol_auditor',
53:                              'app_web', 'admin_datos', 'usr_soporte', 'usr_reportes', 'usr_auditor'] LOOP
54:         EXECUTE format('REVOKE ALL ON ALL TABLES    IN SCHEMA public FROM %I', r);
55:         EXECUTE format('REVOKE ALL ON ALL SEQUENCES IN SCHEMA public FROM %I', r);
56:         EXECUTE format('REVOKE ALL ON ALL ROUTINES  IN SCHEMA public FROM %I', r);
57:         EXECUTE format('REVOKE ALL ON SCHEMA public FROM %I', r);
58:         EXECUTE format('REVOKE ALL ON DATABASE %I FROM %I', current_database(), r);
59:     END LOOP;
60:     -- Los permisos de columna no se van con REVOKE ALL ON ALL TABLES.
61:     EXECUTE 'REVOKE ALL (id, nombre, apellido, mail, celular, contrasena, rol, eliminado, created_at) ON usuario FROM rol_soporte';
62:     EXECUTE 'REVOKE ALL (stock) ON producto FROM rol_app_escritura';
63: END $$;
64: 
65: -- PUBLIC (todos los roles) no se conecta, no usa el esquema y no ejecuta funciones nuevas.
66: DO $$ BEGIN EXECUTE format('REVOKE ALL ON DATABASE %I FROM PUBLIC', current_database()); END $$;
67: REVOKE ALL ON SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC;
68: REVOKE EXECUTE ON ALL ROUTINES IN SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC;
69: 
70: -- 3. Conexión y esquema ------------------------------------------------------------
71: DO $$
72: BEGIN
73:     EXECUTE format('GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE %I TO app_web, admin_datos, usr_soporte, usr_reportes, usr_auditor',
74:                    current_database());
75: END $$;
76: GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO rol_app_lectura, rol_app_escritura, rol_soporte, rol_reportes, rol_auditor, admin_datos;
77: 
78: -- 4. Roles de grupo ------------------------------------------------------------------
79: 
80: -- rol_app_lectura: catálogo y pedidos (sin cliente ni usuario)
81: GRANT SELECT ON categoria, producto, pedido, detalle_pedido, vista_productos_vigentes TO rol_app_lectura;
82: 
83: -- rol_app_escritura: registrar ventas. UPDATE solo sobre la columna stock: la app no cambia precios.
84: GRANT INSERT ON pedido, detalle_pedido TO rol_app_escritura;
85: GRANT UPDATE (stock) ON producto TO rol_app_escritura;
86: GRANT EXECUTE ON PROCEDURE sp_registrar_pedido(BIGINT, forma_pago_enum, JSONB) TO rol_app_escritura;
87: GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION  fn_total_pedido(BIGINT)                            TO rol_app_escritura;
88: 
89: -- rol_soporte: permisos de COLUMNA sobre usuario. Ve todo menos la contraseña y solo
90: -- corrige celular y baja. Para la contraseña usa fn_resetear_password.
91: GRANT SELECT (id, nombre, apellido, mail, celular, rol, eliminado, created_at) ON usuario TO rol_soporte;
92: GRANT UPDATE (celular, eliminado) ON usuario TO rol_soporte;
93: GRANT SELECT ON cliente TO rol_soporte;
94: GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION fn_resetear_password(TEXT, TEXT) TO rol_soporte;
95: 
96: -- rol_reportes: solo vistas y agregados. vista_usuario_reportes (U3) NO se otorga:
97: -- oculta la contraseña, pero expone mail y celular. Para usuarios, usa usuario_anon (Parte D).
98: GRANT SELECT ON mv_facturacion_cat_mes, v_top5_categorias, vista_productos_vigentes,
99:                 vista_detalle_pedido_producto TO rol_reportes;
100: 
101: -- rol_auditor: registros de auditoría.
102: GRANT SELECT ON auditoria_seguridad, auditoria_precio TO rol_auditor;
103: 
104: -- 5. Logins ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
105: GRANT rol_app_lectura, rol_app_escritura TO app_web;
106: GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION fn_autenticar(TEXT, TEXT) TO app_web;     -- solo la app autentica
107: 
108: GRANT rol_soporte  TO usr_soporte;
109: GRANT rol_reportes TO usr_reportes;
110: GRANT rol_auditor  TO usr_auditor;
111: 
112: -- admin_datos: DML completo sobre los datos del esquema. No recibe TRUNCATE, REFERENCES ni
113: -- TRIGGER, no es dueño de los objetos y no tiene ADMIN OPTION sobre ningún rol.
114: GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO admin_datos;
115: -- La auditoría es de solo lectura también para admin_datos (hallazgo #1 de la auditoría con
116: -- OpenCode, comprobado en evidencias/A_04): quien administra los datos no puede borrar ni
117: -- cambiar la evidencia de lo que hizo. Las filas las escriben fn_autenticar y el trigger
118: -- de precios, que son SECURITY DEFINER y corren como su dueño.
119: REVOKE INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON auditoria_seguridad, auditoria_precio FROM admin_datos;
120: GRANT USAGE, SELECT ON ALL SEQUENCES IN SCHEMA public TO admin_datos;
121: GRANT EXECUTE ON ALL ROUTINES IN SCHEMA public TO admin_datos;
122: 
123: -- 6. Objetos futuros -----------------------------------------------------------------------
124: -- Lo que postgres cree de acá en adelante hereda la misma política: nadie recibe acceso
125: -- automático salvo admin_datos, y las funciones nuevas no quedan abiertas a PUBLIC.
126: -- El REVOKE va sin IN SCHEMA: los privilegios por esquema solo se SUMAN a los globales,
127: -- y el EXECUTE a PUBLIC es global. Con IN SCHEMA, el REVOKE no tendría efecto.
128: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE postgres
129:     REVOKE EXECUTE ON ROUTINES FROM PUBLIC;
130: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE postgres IN SCHEMA public
131:     GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON TABLES TO admin_datos;
132: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE postgres IN SCHEMA public
133:     GRANT USAGE, SELECT ON SEQUENCES TO admin_datos;
134: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE postgres IN SCHEMA public
135:     GRANT EXECUTE ON ROUTINES TO admin_datos;

18: IP_CON_PUERTO = re.compile(r"(?<![\w.:])((?:\d{1,3}\.){3}\d{1,3}|[0-9A-Fa-f]{0,4}(?::[0-9A-Fa-f]{0,4}){2,7})\((\d+)\)")
19: # "host=... port=..." de la línea "connection received"
20: HOST = re.compile(r"host=((?:\d{1,3}\.){3}\d{1,3}|[0-9A-Fa-f:]+)")
21: PUERTO = re.compile(r"port=\d+")
22: CLAVE = re.compile(r"((?:fn_autenticar|fn_resetear_password)\(\s*'[^']*'\s*,\s*)'[^']*'")
23: 
24: ips: dict[str, str] = {}
25: 
26: 
27: def alias_ip(ip: str) -> str:
28:     if ip not in ips:
29:         ips[ip] = f"ip_origen_{len(ips) + 1}"
30:     return ips[ip]
31: 
32: 
33: def alias_mail(m: re.Match) -> str:
34:     h = hashlib.sha256((SAL + m.group(0).lower()).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
35:     return f"anon_{h[:10]}@ejemplo.test"
36: 
37: 
38: def anonimizar(linea: str) -> str:
39:     linea = CLAVE.sub(r"\1'***'", linea)
40:     linea = MAIL.sub(alias_mail, linea)
41:     linea = IP_CON_PUERTO.sub(lambda m: f"{alias_ip(m.group(1))}(puerto)", linea)
42:     linea = HOST.sub(lambda m: f"host={alias_ip(m.group(1))}", linea)
43:     linea = PUERTO.sub("port=(puerto)", linea)
44:     return linea
45: 
46: 
47: def main() -> None:
48:     for linea in sys.stdin:
49:         sys.stdout.write(anonimizar(linea))
50: 
51: 
52: if __name__ == "__main__":
53:     main()

1: -- U5 · 01 — Autenticación de la aplicación: fn_autenticar y fn_resetear_password
2: -- Reconstrucción de las funciones de la Clase 2 (no se conservaban en el repositorio).
3: --
4: -- Decisiones:
5: --   * SECURITY DEFINER: corren con los permisos del dueño, así app_web puede validar una
6: --     contraseña sin tener permiso de lectura sobre usuario.contrasena.
7: --   * SET search_path fijo: evita que alguien cree un objeto con el mismo nombre en otro
8: --     esquema y la función lo use (ataque clásico a funciones SECURITY DEFINER).
9: --   * Cada intento queda en auditoria_seguridad (registro de rendición de cuentas) y,
10: --     además, en el log del servidor con RAISE LOG (registro técnico).
11: --   * EXECUTE se revoca de PUBLIC: por defecto, cualquier rol puede ejecutar una función.
12: --   * SET log_min_error_statement = 'panic': para el log del servidor, el nivel LOG está por
13: --     encima de ERROR, así que cada RAISE LOG agregaba la línea STATEMENT con la llamada
14: --     completa, es decir, con la contraseña en texto plano. Se detectó al probar el
15: --     simulacro (ver BITACORA.md). Con este ajuste, solo dentro de estas funciones, el log
16: --     registra el evento sin la sentencia.
17: 
18: CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgcrypto;
19: 
20: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS auditoria_seguridad (
21:     id          BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
22:     momento     TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp(),
23:     evento      TEXT        NOT NULL CHECK (evento IN ('LOGIN', 'RESET_PASSWORD')),
24:     exito       BOOLEAN     NOT NULL,
25:     mail        TEXT        NOT NULL,
26:     usuario_id  BIGINT,
27:     rol_bd      TEXT        NOT NULL DEFAULT session_user,
28:     origen      INET                 DEFAULT inet_client_addr()
29: );
30: 
31: -- Devuelve el usuario si el mail y la contraseña coinciden; si no, ninguna fila.
32: -- No distingue "mail inexistente" de "contraseña incorrecta" para no revelar qué mails existen.
33: CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION fn_autenticar(p_mail TEXT, p_contrasena TEXT)
34: RETURNS TABLE (usuario_id BIGINT, nombre TEXT, rol TEXT)
35: LANGUAGE plpgsql
36: SECURITY DEFINER
37: SET search_path = public, pg_temp
38: SET log_min_error_statement = 'panic'
39: AS $$
40: DECLARE
41:     v_id     BIGINT;
42:     v_nombre TEXT;
43:     v_rol    TEXT;
44:     v_hash   TEXT;
45: BEGIN
46:     SELECT u.id, u.nombre, u.rol::TEXT, u.contrasena
47:       INTO v_id, v_nombre, v_rol, v_hash
48:       FROM usuario u
49:      WHERE lower(u.mail) = lower(p_mail) AND NOT u.eliminado;
50: 
51:     -- Solo se comparan hashes bcrypt; las contraseñas heredadas en otro formato no validan.
52:     IF v_hash LIKE '$2%' AND crypt(p_contrasena, v_hash) = v_hash THEN
53:         INSERT INTO auditoria_seguridad (evento, exito, mail, usuario_id)
54:         VALUES ('LOGIN', TRUE, p_mail, v_id);
55:         RAISE LOG 'fn_autenticar: inicio de sesion correcto mail=% usuario_id=%', p_mail, v_id;
56:         RETURN QUERY SELECT v_id, v_nombre, v_rol;
57:     ELSE
58:         INSERT INTO auditoria_seguridad (evento, exito, mail, usuario_id)
59:         VALUES ('LOGIN', FALSE, p_mail, v_id);
60:         RAISE LOG 'fn_autenticar: intento fallido mail=%', p_mail;
61:     END IF;
62: END $$;
63: 
64: -- Reemplaza la contraseña de un usuario. Reservada a soporte.
65: CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION fn_resetear_password(p_mail TEXT, p_nueva TEXT)
66: RETURNS BOOLEAN
67: LANGUAGE plpgsql
68: SECURITY DEFINER
69: SET search_path = public, pg_temp
70: SET log_min_error_statement = 'panic'
71: AS $$
72: DECLARE
73:     v_id BIGINT;
74: BEGIN
75:     IF length(p_nueva) < 10 THEN
76:         RAISE EXCEPTION 'La contraseña nueva debe tener al menos 10 caracteres';
77:     END IF;
78: 
79:     UPDATE usuario
80:        SET contrasena = crypt(p_nueva, gen_salt('bf', 10))
81:      WHERE lower(mail) = lower(p_mail) AND NOT eliminado
82:     RETURNING id INTO v_id;
83: 
84:     INSERT INTO auditoria_seguridad (evento, exito, mail, usuario_id)
85:     VALUES ('RESET_PASSWORD', v_id IS NOT NULL, p_mail, v_id);
86:     RAISE LOG 'fn_resetear_password: mail=% exito=%', p_mail, v_id IS NOT NULL;
87:     RETURN v_id IS NOT NULL;
88: END $$;
89: 
90: REVOKE ALL ON FUNCTION fn_autenticar(TEXT, TEXT)        FROM PUBLIC;
91: REVOKE ALL ON FUNCTION fn_resetear_password(TEXT, TEXT) FROM PUBLIC;
92: 
93: -- Funciones de trigger que escriben tablas internas (auditoría de precios de la U3 y
94: -- resumen de ventas de la U4). Si corrieran con los permisos de quien vende, habría que
95: -- darle a app_web permiso de escritura sobre esas tablas. Corriendo como dueño, no.
96: ALTER FUNCTION fn_auditar_precios()          SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path = public, pg_temp;
97: ALTER FUNCTION fn_resumen_detalle()          SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path = public, pg_temp;
98: ALTER FUNCTION fn_resumen_cambio_categoria() SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path = public, pg_temp;

_Thinking:_

Now more confirmations:

- `respaldo_tarea.cmd` line 8: `cd %CD:\=/%` no quotes. If path has spaces, bash -c argument is `"cd C:/Users/.../unidad6_mantenimiento && ./backup_foodstore.sh"`. Actually the whole -c argument is quoted with double quotes: `-l -c "cd %CD:\=/% && ./backup_foodstore.sh"`. Inside, `cd C:/Users/moran/BD2/tpi-food-store/trabajos-practicos/unidad6_mantenimiento` — if path has spaces, bash's `cd` gets split. So yes, breaks with spaces. The current path has no spaces (`moran`), so works in this environment. Real portability bug. Also line 9: `echo codigo de salida: %errorlevel%` — in cmd, `%errorlevel%` is expanded at parse time of the line; but since it's a separate line after the bash call, it should reflect the bash exit code. Actually in a batch file, each line is parsed when executed, so `%errorlevel%` expands to the current value at execution → correct. But the script's final exit code is the exit code of `echo` (0), not the bash exit code. So scheduled task reports success even if backup failed. Confirmed. Real.

- `programar_respaldo.cmd`: line 10 `schtasks /Run` does not wait or check. Confirmed. Real-ish. Also line 4 for /TR quoting — seems okay. Also it uses `schtasks /Run` which runs asynchronously. So can't verify. Minor.

- `restore_test.sh`: line 40 `pg_restore --no-owner --no-privileges`. This means roles/ownership/privileges aren't restored, so restore test does not validate GRANTs or ownership. Also backup_foodstore.sh uses pg_dump (not pg_dumpall), so globals/roles not backed up. So a real disaster recovery using these backups would not recreate roles (app_web, etc.). Confirmed. Also validation only 5 tables. But note line 82 checks `ok_filas` and `invalidos`, and line 90 greps "Validaciones: OK" and exits non-zero if not. Good. But note: line 40 with `--exit-on-error` means pg_restore errors abort (set -e). Fine. Also line 50 uses `/tmp/conteos_restaurada.txt` — on Windows Git Bash `/tmp` exists. Fine.

Wait, another subtle bug in restore_test.sh: line 54 `while read -r tabla n_resp; do ... done < "$conteos"`. The `conteos` file lines might have `\r` at the end (from psql on Windows). n_resp strips `\r` via `${n_resp//$'\r'/}`. Good. tabela name is first field, no `\r`. Fine.

Another subtle: `pg_restore --no-owner` means objects will be owned by the restoring user (postgres), and owner-based privileges change. Combined with `--no-privileges`, grants not restored. So the test can't catch permission regressions. That's the finding.

- `backup_foodstore.sh`: uses `pg_dump -Fc` (only the DB, not globals). No roles backup. Confirmed. Also line 41: `pg_restore --list "$dump" | grep -vc '^;'` — with `set -o pipefail`, if grep finds zero non-comment lines it returns 1 → triggers error. Fine (empty dump is bad). But note pipefail + grep -vc: if grep exits 1 because count 0, the `if !` catches. Fine.

Also `backup_foodstore.sh` registers but does not include `auditoria_seguridad`, `auditoria_precio`, `usuario_anon` etc. Actually pg_dump includes all tables. The conteos only 5 tables but backup includes all. Fine.

1: // U7 · Carga de los pedidos exportados desde PostgreSQL en MongoDB
2: // Uso (desde esta carpeta): mongosh "mongodb://localhost:27017" --file cargar_mongodb.js
3: // Con Atlas: mongosh "mongodb+srv://..." --file cargar_mongodb.js
4: //
5: // Reglas de integridad que se conservan en la migración:
6: //   R1. total = suma de cantidad × precio_unitario de sus líneas, al centavo.
7: //       Se controla antes de insertar: si un documento no cumple, no se carga ninguno.
8: //   R2. Cada línea tiene cantidad entera > 0 y precio_unitario >= 0, y todo pedido tiene
9: //       al menos una línea. Lo hace cumplir el validador $jsonSchema de la colección,
10: //       también para lo que se inserte después.
11: 
12: const fs = require('fs');
13: 
14: db = db.getSiblingDB('foodstore');
15: 
16: const ESTADOS = ['PENDIENTE', 'CONFIRMADO', 'ENTREGADO', 'CANCELADO'];
17: const FORMAS_PAGO = ['EFECTIVO', 'TARJETA', 'TRANSFERENCIA'];
18: 
19: // '2200.00' -> 220000 centavos, sin pasar por punto flotante
20: function centavos(texto) {
21:   const [entero, dec = ''] = texto.split('.');
22:   return parseInt(entero, 10) * 100 + parseInt((dec + '00').slice(0, 2), 10);
23: }
24: const dinero = (texto) => Decimal128.fromString(texto);
25: 
26: const origen = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync('pedidos_export.json', 'utf8'));
27: print(`Documentos leídos de pedidos_export.json: ${origen.length}`);
28: 
29: // R1: control del total antes de convertir nada
30: const errores = origen.filter((p) =>
31:   p.lineas.reduce((s, l) => s + l.cantidad * centavos(l.precio_unitario), 0) !== centavos(p.total));
32: if (errores.length > 0) {
33:   throw new Error(`R1 no se cumple en los pedidos ${errores.map((p) => p._id).join(', ')}: no se carga nada`);
34: }
35: 
36: const documentos = origen.map((p) => ({
37:   _id: p._id,                                   // id_pedido de PostgreSQL
38:   fecha: new Date(p.fecha),
39:   estado: p.estado,

<type>file</type>
<content>
1: -- U4 · 06 — Desnormalización controlada: resumen de ventas por categoría
2: --
3: -- Consulta que se quiere acelerar: el top 5 de categorías por facturación.
4: -- Normalizada, recorre todo detalle_pedido y lo une con producto y categoría.
5: -- La tabla resumen guarda esos totales ya calculados.
6: --
7: -- Salvaguardas:
8: --   1. Triggers que actualizan el resumen en la MISMA transacción que la venta.
9: --   2. fn_verificar_resumen_categoria(): compara el resumen con el cálculo real.
10: --   3. sp_recalcular_resumen_categoria(): reconstruye el resumen si alguna vez difiere.
11: --   4. CHECK de no negatividad: un descuento mal hecho da error en vez de un total absurdo.
12: --   5. Reversión documentada en 07_reversion_desnormalizacion.sql.
13: 
14: DROP VIEW    IF EXISTS v_top5_categorias;
15: DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS trg_resumen_detalle_ins ON detalle_pedido;
16: DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS trg_resumen_detalle_upd ON detalle_pedido;
17: DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS trg_resumen_detalle_del ON detalle_pedido;
18: DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS trg_resumen_cambio_categoria ON producto;
19: DROP TABLE   IF EXISTS resumen_ventas_categoria CASCADE;
20: 
21: CREATE TABLE resumen_ventas_categoria (
22:     id_categoria    BIGINT        PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES categoria (id_categoria),
23:     unidades        BIGINT        NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (unidades >= 0),
24:     facturacion     NUMERIC(16,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (facturacion >= 0),
25:     actualizado_en  TIMESTAMPTZ   NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
26: );
27: 
28: COMMENT ON TABLE resumen_ventas_categoria IS
29:   'Desnormalización controlada (U4): totales por categoría mantenidos por triggers sobre detalle_pedido y producto.';
30: 
31: -- Aplica un conjunto de variaciones (id_categoria, unidades, facturación) al resumen.
32: -- Primero actualiza las categorías que ya tienen fila y después inserta las nuevas.
33: -- No se usa un único INSERT ... ON CONFLICT: PostgreSQL controla los CHECK sobre la fila
34: -- propuesta antes de detectar el conflicto, y una variación negativa (una venta que se
35: -- borra) haría fallar el CHECK aunque el total final sea válido.
36: CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION fn_resumen_aplicar(p_delta JSONB)
37: RETURNS VOID
38: LANGUAGE sql AS $$
39:     WITH d AS (
40:         SELECT (e->>'id_categoria')::BIGINT AS id_categoria,
41:                (e->>'unidades')::BIGINT     AS unidades,
42:                (e->>'facturacion')::NUMERIC AS facturacion
43:           FROM jsonb_array_elements(p_delta) AS e
44:     ), upd AS (
45:         UPDATE resumen_ventas_categoria r
46:            SET unidades       = r.unidades    + d.unidades,
47:                facturacion    = r.facturacion + d.facturacion,
48:                actualizado_en = now()
49:           FROM d
50:          WHERE r.id_categoria = d.id_categoria
51:         RETURNING r.id_categoria
52:     )
53:     INSERT INTO resumen_ventas_categoria AS r (id_categoria, unidades, facturacion)
54:     SELECT d.id_categoria, d.unidades, d.facturacion
55:       FROM d
56:      WHERE d.id_categoria NOT IN (SELECT id_categoria FROM upd)
57:     ON CONFLICT (id_categoria) DO UPDATE      -- otra transacción insertó la misma categoría a la vez
58:        SET unidades       = r.unidades    + EXCLUDED.unidades,
59:            facturacion    = r.facturacion + EXCLUDED.facturacion,
60:            actualizado_en = now();
61: $$;
62: 
63: -- Trigger por sentencia sobre detalle_pedido: usa tablas de transición, así un INSERT
64: -- de muchas líneas actualiza el resumen una sola vez.
65: CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION fn_resumen_detalle()
66: RETURNS TRIGGER
67: LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
68: DECLARE
69:     v_delta JSONB;
70: BEGIN
71:     IF TG_OP = 'INSERT' THEN
72:         SELECT jsonb_agg(x) INTO v_delta FROM (
73:             SELECT p.id_categoria, SUM(n.cantidad) AS unidades, SUM(n.cantidad * n.precio_unitario) AS facturacion
74:               FROM nuevas n JOIN producto p ON p.id_producto = n.id_producto
75:              GROUP BY p.id_categoria) x;
76:     ELSIF TG_OP = 'DELETE' THEN
77:         SELECT jsonb_agg(x) INTO v_delta FROM (
78:             SELECT p.id_categoria, -SUM(o.cantidad) AS unidades, -SUM(o.cantidad * o.precio_unitario) AS facturacion
79:               FROM viejas o JOIN producto p ON p.id_producto = o.id_producto
80:              GROUP BY p.id_categoria) x;
81:     ELSE  -- UPDATE
82:         SELECT jsonb_agg(x) INTO v_delta FROM (
83:             SELECT id_categoria, SUM(unidades) AS unidades, SUM(facturacion) AS facturacion
84:               FROM (SELECT p.id_categoria, n.cantidad AS unidades, n.cantidad * n.precio_unitario AS facturacion
85:                       FROM nuevas n JOIN producto p ON p.id_producto = n.id_producto
86:                     UNION ALL
87:                     SELECT p.id_categoria, -o.cantidad, -(o.cantidad * o.precio_unitario)
88:                       FROM viejas o JOIN producto p ON p.id_producto = o.id_producto) t
89:              GROUP BY id_categoria) x;
90:     END IF;
91:     IF v_delta IS NOT NULL THEN
92:         PERFORM fn_resumen_aplicar(v_delta);
93:     END IF;
94:     RETURN NULL;
95: END $$;
96: 
97: -- PostgreSQL no admite tablas de transición en un trigger con varios eventos: van tres.
98: CREATE TRIGGER trg_resumen_detalle_ins AFTER INSERT ON detalle_pedido
99:     REFERENCING NEW TABLE AS nuevas
100:     FOR EACH STATEMENT EXECUTE FUNCTION fn_resumen_detalle();
101: CREATE TRIGGER trg_resumen_detalle_upd AFTER UPDATE ON detalle_pedido
102:     REFERENCING OLD TABLE AS viejas NEW TABLE AS nuevas
103:     FOR EACH STATEMENT EXECUTE FUNCTION fn_resumen_detalle();
104: CREATE TRIGGER trg_resumen_detalle_del AFTER DELETE ON detalle_pedido
105:     REFERENCING OLD TABLE AS viejas
106:     FOR EACH STATEMENT EXECUTE FUNCTION fn_resumen_detalle();
107: 
108: -- Si un producto cambia de categoría, sus ventas pasan a la categoría nueva.
109: CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION fn_resumen_cambio_categoria()
110: RETURNS TRIGGER
111: LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
112: DECLARE
113:     v_u BIGINT;
114:     v_f NUMERIC;
115: BEGIN
116:     SELECT COALESCE(SUM(cantidad), 0), COALESCE(SUM(cantidad * precio_unitario), 0)
117:       INTO v_u, v_f
118:       FROM detalle_pedido WHERE id_producto = NEW.id_producto;
119:     IF v_u > 0 THEN
120:         PERFORM fn_resumen_aplicar(jsonb_build_array(
121:             jsonb_build_object('id_categoria', OLD.id_categoria, 'unidades', -v_u, 'facturacion', -v_f),
122:             jsonb_build_object('id_categoria', NEW.id_categoria, 'unidades',  v_u, 'facturacion',  v_f)));
123:     END IF;
124:     RETURN NULL;
125: END $$;
126: 
127: CREATE TRIGGER trg_resumen_cambio_categoria
128:     AFTER UPDATE OF id_categoria ON producto
129:     FOR EACH ROW WHEN (OLD.id_categoria IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.id_categoria)
130:     EXECUTE FUNCTION fn_resumen_cambio_categoria();
131: 
132: -- Salvaguarda 2: diferencias entre el resumen y el cálculo real (vacío = consistente).
133: CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION fn_verificar_resumen_categoria()
134: RETURNS TABLE (id_categoria BIGINT, unidades_resumen BIGINT, unidades_real BIGINT,
135:                facturacion_resumen NUMERIC, facturacion_real NUMERIC)
136: LANGUAGE sql STABLE AS $$
137:     WITH real AS (
138:         SELECT c.id_categoria,
139:                COALESCE(SUM(dp.cantidad), 0)::BIGINT                   AS unidades,
140:                COALESCE(SUM(dp.cantidad * dp.precio_unitario), 0)      AS facturacion
141:           FROM categoria c
142:           LEFT JOIN producto p        ON p.id_categoria = c.id_categoria
143:           LEFT JOIN detalle_pedido dp ON dp.id_producto = p.id_producto
144:          GROUP BY c.id_categoria)
145:     SELECT real.id_categoria, r.unidades, real.unidades, r.facturacion, real.facturacion
146:       FROM real
147:       LEFT JOIN resumen_ventas_categoria r ON r.id_categoria = real.id_categoria
148:      WHERE r.id_categoria IS NULL
149:         OR r.unidades    <> real.unidades
150:         OR r.facturacion <> real.facturacion;
151: $$;
152: 
153: -- Salvaguarda 3: reconstrucción completa.
154: CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE sp_recalcular_resumen_categoria()
155: LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
156: BEGIN
157:     LOCK TABLE resumen_ventas_categoria IN EXCLUSIVE MODE;
158:     DELETE FROM resumen_ventas_categoria;
159:     INSERT INTO resumen_ventas_categoria (id_categoria, unidades, facturacion)
160:     SELECT c.id_categoria,
161:            COALESCE(SUM(dp.cantidad), 0),
162:            COALESCE(SUM(dp.cantidad * dp.precio_unitario), 0)
163:       FROM categoria c
164:       LEFT JOIN producto p        ON p.id_categoria = c.id_categoria
165:       LEFT JOIN detalle_pedido dp ON dp.id_producto = p.id_producto
166:      GROUP BY c.id_categoria;
167: END $$;
168: 
169: -- Carga inicial
170: CALL sp_recalcular_resumen_categoria();
171: 
172: -- Vista del top 5, para que los reportes no dependan del nombre de la tabla.
173: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_top5_categorias AS
174: SELECT c.id_categoria, c.nombre, r.unidades, r.facturacion
175:   FROM resumen_ventas_categoria r
176:   JOIN categoria c ON c.id_categoria = r.id_categoria
177:  ORDER BY r.facturacion DESC
178:  LIMIT 5;

<content>
1: -- U7 · 02 — Exportación de pedidos y detalles a JSON para MongoDB
2: --
3: -- Subconjunto migrado: los pedidos que tienen al menos una línea de un producto del
4: -- catálogo semilla (los 10 productos de sql/02_data.sql). Son pedidos existentes, con
5: -- sus líneas completas. La vista v_pedidos_migrados_mongo fija ese criterio, y
6: -- consultas_postgresql.sql lo usa para comparar contra los mismos pedidos.
7: --
8: -- Decisiones del documento:
9: --   * _id = id_pedido: se conserva el identificador de origen.
10: --   * Importes como texto ('2200.00') para cargarlos en MongoDB como Decimal128, sin
11: --     pasar por un número de punto flotante.
12: --   * Precio histórico: cada línea lleva precio_unitario de detalle_pedido (el de la venta),
13: --     no el precio actual del producto.
14: --   * Del cliente viajan solo id, nombre y apellido: el mail y el teléfono no hacen falta
15: --     para mostrar un pedido (minimización de datos personales).
16: 
17: -- El archivo se escribe en la codificación del cliente: se fija UTF-8 (mongosh lo lee así).
18: \encoding UTF8
19: 
20: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_pedidos_migrados_mongo AS
21: SELECT DISTINCT dp.id_pedido
22:   FROM detalle_pedido dp
23:  WHERE dp.id_producto IN (SELECT id_producto FROM producto
24:                            WHERE nombre IN ('Pan de campo 1kg', 'Medialunas x6', 'Agua mineral 2L',
25:                                             'Gaseosa cola 2.25L', 'Leche entera 1L', 'Queso cremoso 500g',
26:                                             'Yerba mate 1kg', 'Aceite girasol 900ml', 'Fideos secos 500g',
27:                                             'Helado 1L'));
28: 
29: \echo '== Pedidos que se exportan'
30: SELECT COUNT(*) AS pedidos, MIN(id_pedido) AS primero, MAX(id_pedido) AS ultimo FROM v_pedidos_migrados_mongo;
31: 
32: \set QUIET on
33: \pset tuples_only on
34: \pset format unaligned
35: \o pedidos_export.json
36: SELECT jsonb_pretty(jsonb_agg(doc ORDER BY (doc->>'_id')::BIGINT))
37:   FROM (
38:     SELECT jsonb_build_object(
39:              '_id',        p.id_pedido,
40:              'fecha',      to_char(p.fecha AT TIME ZONE 'UTC', 'YYYY-MM-DD"T"HH24:MI:SS.MS"Z"'),
41:              'estado',     p.estado,
42:              'forma_pago', p.forma_pago,
43:              'cliente',    jsonb_build_object('id_cliente', c.id_cliente, 'nombre', c.nombre, 'apellido', c.apellido),
44:              'lineas',     l.lineas,
45:              'total',      l.total::TEXT
46:            ) AS doc
47:       FROM pedido p
48:       JOIN cliente c ON c.id_cliente = p.id_cliente
49:       JOIN LATERAL (
50:             SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(
51:                        'id_detalle',      dp.id_detalle,
52:                        'id_producto',     dp.id_producto,
53:                        'producto',        pr.nombre,
54:                        'categoria',       ca.nombre,
55:                        'cantidad',        dp.cantidad,
56:                        'precio_unitario', dp.precio_unitario::TEXT,
57:                        'subtotal',        (dp.cantidad * dp.precio_unitario)::TEXT)
58:                      ORDER BY dp.id_detalle) AS lineas,
59:                    SUM(dp.cantidad * dp.precio_unitario) AS total
60:               FROM detalle_pedido dp
61:               JOIN producto  pr ON pr.id_producto  = dp.id_producto
62:               JOIN categoria ca ON ca.id_categoria = pr.id_categoria
63:              WHERE dp.id_pedido = p.id_pedido) l ON TRUE
64:      WHERE p.id_pedido IN (SELECT id_pedido FROM v_pedidos_migrados_mongo)
65:   ) docs;
66: \o
67: \pset tuples_only off
68: \pset format aligned
69: \set QUIET off
70: \echo '== Archivo generado: pedidos_export.json'

(End of file - total 70 lines)
</content>

6:   FROM pedido p

25:  WHERE p.id_pedido IN (SELECT id_pedido FROM v_pedidos_migrados_mongo)
26:    AND pr.nombre = 'Yerba mate 1kg'
27:  ORDER BY p.id_pedido;
28: SELECT COUNT(*) AS cantidad, array_agg(p.id_pedido ORDER BY p.id_pedido) AS ids
29:   FROM pedido p

32:                 WHERE dp.id_pedido = p.id_pedido AND pr.nombre = 'Yerba mate 1kg');
33: 
34: \echo '== d) Pedidos con total superior al ticket promedio del subconjunto'
35: WITH totales AS (
36:     SELECT dp.id_pedido, SUM(dp.cantidad * dp.precio_unitario) AS total
37:       FROM detalle_pedido dp
38:      WHERE dp.id_pedido IN (SELECT id_pedido FROM v_pedidos_migrados_mongo)
39:      GROUP BY dp.id_pedido)
40: SELECT ROUND(AVG(total), 2) AS umbral,
41:        COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE total > (SELECT ROUND(AVG(total), 2) FROM totales)) AS cantidad,
42:        array_agg(id_pedido ORDER BY id_pedido) FILTER (WHERE total > (SELECT ROUND(AVG(total), 2) FROM totales)) AS ids
43:   FROM totales;

<path>C:\Users\moran\BD2\tpi-food-store\trabajos-practicos\unidad4_fnbc_desnormalizacion\sql\03_migracion_fnbc.sql</path>
<type>file</type>
<content>
1: -- U4 · 03 — Migración a BCNF dentro de una transacción reversible
2: --
3: -- Descompone control_lote_almacen (L, D, R) por la DF violatoria R -> D:
4: --   R1 = responsable_deposito (R, D)   clave: R
5: --   R2 = control_lote         (L, R)   clave: {L, R}
6: --
7: -- Uso:
8: --   psql -d foodstore -f 03_migracion_fnbc.sql                    -> ensayo: corre todo y termina en ROLLBACK
9: --   psql -d foodstore -v accion=COMMIT -f 03_migracion_fnbc.sql   -> aplica la migración
10: -- Si cualquier verificación falla, el script se corta y no queda nada a medias.
11: 
12: \set ON_ERROR_STOP on
13: \if :{?accion}
14: \else
15:   \set accion ROLLBACK
16: \endif
17: \echo '== Modo de ejecución:' :accion
18: 
19: BEGIN;
20: 
21: -- 0. Precondiciones: la tabla heredada existe y la DF2 se cumple en los datos.
22: DO $$
23: BEGIN
24:     IF to_regclass('public.control_lote_almacen') IS NULL THEN
25:         RAISE EXCEPTION 'No existe la tabla heredada control_lote_almacen (¿ya se migró?)';
26:     END IF;
27:     IF EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM control_lote_almacen
28:                 GROUP BY responsable_control_id
29:                HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT deposito_id) > 1) THEN
30:         RAISE EXCEPTION 'La DF responsable -> depósito no se cumple en los datos: corregirlos antes de migrar';
31:     END IF;
32: END $$;
33: 
34: -- 1. R1: un responsable pertenece a un único depósito (la PK garantiza R -> D).
35: CREATE TABLE responsable_deposito (
36:     responsable_control_id  BIGINT PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES usuario (id),
37:     deposito_id             BIGINT NOT NULL    REFERENCES deposito (id)
38: );
39: CREATE INDEX idx_responsable_deposito_deposito ON responsable_deposito (deposito_id);
40: 
41: -- 2. R2: qué responsable controló cada lote.
42: CREATE TABLE control_lote (
43:     lote_id                 BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES lote (id),
44:     responsable_control_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES responsable_deposito (responsable_control_id),
45:     PRIMARY KEY (lote_id, responsable_control_id)
46: );
47: CREATE INDEX idx_control_lote_responsable ON control_lote (responsable_control_id);
48: 
49: -- 3. Carga sin pérdida desde la tabla heredada.
50: INSERT INTO responsable_deposito (responsable_control_id, deposito_id)
51: SELECT DISTINCT responsable_control_id, deposito_id FROM control_lote_almacen;
52: 
53: INSERT INTO control_lote (lote_id, responsable_control_id)
54: SELECT lote_id, responsable_control_id FROM control_lote_almacen;
55: 
56: -- 4. La tabla original se conserva como respaldo y una vista reconstruye la relación.
57: ALTER TABLE control_lote_almacen RENAME TO control_lote_almacen_respaldo;
58: 
59: CREATE VIEW v_control_lote_almacen AS
60: SELECT cl.lote_id, rd.deposito_id, cl.responsable_control_id
61:   FROM control_lote cl
62:   JOIN responsable_deposito rd ON rd.responsable_control_id = cl.responsable_control_id;
63: 
64: -- 5. Salvaguarda de la DF1 {L, D} -> R.
65: -- La descomposición en BCNF no preserva esta dependencia: ninguna de las dos tablas
66: -- tiene L y D juntos. Sin esta salvaguarda, dos responsables del mismo depósito
67: -- podrían controlar el mismo lote. El candado serializa a los escritores para que
68: -- dos transacciones concurrentes no pasen el control a la vez.
69: CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION fn_control_lote_df1()
70: RETURNS TRIGGER
71: LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
72: DECLARE
73:     v_lote BIGINT;
74:     v_dep  BIGINT;
75: BEGIN
76:     PERFORM pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('control_lote_df1'));
77:     SELECT lote_id, deposito_id INTO v_lote, v_dep
78:       FROM v_control_lote_almacen
79:      GROUP BY lote_id, deposito_id
80:     HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
81:      LIMIT 1;
82:     IF FOUND THEN
83:         RAISE EXCEPTION 'El lote % ya tiene un responsable del depósito % (regla {lote, depósito} -> responsable)',
84:                         v_lote, v_dep;
85:     END IF;
86:     RETURN NULL;
87: END $$;
88: 
89: CREATE TRIGGER trg_control_lote_df1
90:     AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE ON control_lote
91:     FOR EACH STATEMENT EXECUTE FUNCTION fn_control_lote_df1();
92: 
93: CREATE TRIGGER trg_responsable_deposito_df1
94:     AFTER UPDATE OF deposito_id ON responsable_deposito
95:     FOR EACH STATEMENT EXECUTE FUNCTION fn_control_lote_df1();
96: 
97: -- 6. Verificación: la reunión devuelve exactamente las filas originales.
98: \echo '== Conteos'
99: SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM control_lote_almacen_respaldo) AS filas_originales,
100:        (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM responsable_deposito)          AS filas_r1,
101:        (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM control_lote)                  AS filas_r2,
102:        (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM v_control_lote_almacen)        AS filas_reunion;
103: 
104: \echo '== Diferencias entre la tabla original y la reunión (se espera 0 y 0)'
105: SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT * FROM control_lote_almacen_respaldo
106:                               EXCEPT SELECT * FROM v_control_lote_almacen) x) AS tuplas_perdidas,
107:        (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT * FROM v_control_lote_almacen
108:                               EXCEPT SELECT * FROM control_lote_almacen_respaldo) x) AS tuplas_espurias;
109: 
110: DO $$
111: DECLARE
112:     v_perdidas INT;
113:     v_espurias INT;
114: BEGIN
115:     SELECT COUNT(*) INTO v_perdidas FROM (SELECT * FROM control_lote_almacen_respaldo
116:                                           EXCEPT SELECT * FROM v_control_lote_almacen) x;
117:     SELECT COUNT(*) INTO v_espurias FROM (SELECT * FROM v_control_lote_almacen
118:                                           EXCEPT SELECT * FROM control_lote_almacen_respaldo) x;
119:     IF v_perdidas + v_espurias > 0 THEN
120:         RAISE EXCEPTION 'La migración no es sin pérdida: % perdidas, % espurias', v_perdidas, v_espurias;
121:     END IF;
122:     RAISE NOTICE 'Verificación sin pérdida: OK';
123: END $$;
124: 
125: :accion;
126: 
127: \echo '== Estado después de' :accion
128: SELECT to_regclass('public.control_lote_almacen')          AS tabla_heredada,
129:        to_regclass('public.control_lote_almacen_respaldo') AS respaldo,
130:        to_regclass('public.responsable_deposito')          AS r1,
131:        to_regclass('public.control_lote')                  AS r2;

Log Message:
-----------
Fix psql \d commands to behave properly when a pattern using regex | is given.
Formerly they'd emit '^foo|bar$' which is wrong because the anchors are
parsed as part of the alternatives; must emit '^(foo|bar)$' to get expected
behavior.  Same as bug found previously in similar_escape().  Already fixed
in HEAD, this is just back-porting the part of that patch that was a bug fix.

Title: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: psql
URL: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/app-psql.html
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
Inside the crosstab grid, for each distinct value `x` of `colH` and each distinct value `y` of `colV`, the cell located at the intersection `(x,y)` contains the value of the `colD` column in the query result row for which the value of `colH` is `x` and the value of `colV` is `y`. If there is no such row, the cell is empty. If there are multiple such rows, an error is reported.
`\d[Sx+] [ pattern ]`#
: For each relation (table, view, materialized view, index, sequence, or foreign table) or composite type matching the `pattern`, show all columns, their types, the tablespace (if not the default) and any special attributes such as `NOT NULL` or defaults. Associated indexes, constraints, rules, and triggers are also shown. For foreign tables, the associated foreign server is shown as well. (“ Matching the pattern” is defined in Patterns below.)

For some types of relation, `\d` shows additional information for each column: column values for sequences, indexed expressions for indexes, and foreign data wrapper options for foreign tables.

The command form `\d+` is identical, except that more information is displayed: any comments associated with the columns of the table are shown, as is the presence of OIDs in the table, the view definition if the relation is a view, a non-default replica identity setting and the access method name if the relation has an access method.

By default, only user-created objects are shown; supply a pattern or the `S` modifier to include system objects.

### Note

If `\d` is used without a `pattern` argument, it is equivalent to `\dtvmsE` which will show a list of all visible tables, views, materialized views, sequences and foreign tables. This is purely a convenience measure.

As with many other commands, if `x` is appended to the command name, the results are displayed in expanded mode, but note that this only applies when `\d` is used without a `pattern` argument, and the `x` modifier cannot appear immediately after the `\d` (because `\dx` is a different command); the `x` modifier may only appear after an `S` or `+` modifier. For example, `\d+x` is equivalent to `\dtvmsE+x` and will show a list of all relations in expanded mode.
`\da[Sx] [ pattern ]`#
: Lists aggregate functions, together with their return type and the data types they operate on. If `pattern` is specified, only aggregates whose names match the pattern are shown. By default, only user-created objects are shown; supply a pattern or the `S` modifier to include system objects. If `x` is appended to the command name, the results are displayed in expanded mode.

...

If `+` is appended to the command name, each access method is listed with its associated handler function and description.
`\dAc[x+] [access-method-pattern [input-type-pattern]]`#
: Lists operator classes (see Section 36.16.1).

...

If ... If `x` is appended to the command name, the results are displayed in expanded mode. If `+` is appended to the command name, functions are displayed verbosely, with their actual parameter lists.
`\db[x+] [ pattern ]`#
: Lists tablespaces. If `pattern` is specified, only tablespaces whose names match the pattern are shown. If `x` is appended to the command name, the results are displayed in expanded mode. If `+` is appended to the command name, each tablespace is listed with its associated options, on-disk size, permissions and description.

...

#### Patterns

The various `\d` commands accept a `pattern` parameter to specify the object name(s) to be displayed. In the simplest case, a pattern is just the exact name of the object. The characters within a pattern are normally folded to lower case, just as in SQL names; for example, `\dt FOO` will display the table named `foo`. As in SQL names, placing double quotes around a pattern stops folding to lower case. Should you need to include an actual double quote character in a pattern, write it as a pair of double quotes within a double-quote sequence; again this is in accord with the rules for SQL quoted identifiers. For example, `\dt "FOO""BAR"` will display the table named `FOO"BAR` (not `foo"bar`). Unlike the normal rules for SQL names, you can put double quotes around just part of a pattern, for instance `\dt FOO"FOO"BAR` will display the table named `fooFOObar`.

Whenever the `pattern` parameter is omitted completely, the `\d` commands display all objects that are visible in the current schema search path — this is equivalent to using `*` as the pattern. (An object is said to be visible if its containing schema is in the search path and no object of the same kind and name appears earlier in the search path. This is equivalent to the statement that the object can be referenced by name without explicit schema qualification.) To see all objects in the database regardless of visibility, use `*.*` as the pattern.

Within a pattern, `*` matches any sequence of characters (including no characters) and `?` matches any single character. (This notation is comparable to Unix shell file name patterns.) For example, `\dt int*` displays tables whose names begin with `int`. But within double quotes, `*` and `?` lose these special meanings and are just matched literally.

...

Advanced users can use regular-expression notations such as character classes, for example `[0-9]` to match any digit. All regular expression special characters work as specified in Section 9.7.3, except for `.` which is taken as a separator as mentioned above, `*` which is translated to the regular-expression notation `.*`, `?` which is translated to `.`, and `$` which is matched literally. You can emulate these pattern characters at need by writing `?` for `.`, `(R+|)` for `R*`, or `(R|)` for `R?`. `$` is not needed as a regular-expression character since the pattern must match the whole name, unlike the usual interpretation of regular expressions (in other words, `$` is automatically appended to your pattern). Write `*` at the beginning and/or end if you don't wish the pattern to be anchored. Note that within double quotes, all regular expression special characters lose their special meanings and are matched literally. Also, the regular expression special characters are matched literally in operator name patterns (i.e., the argument of `\do`).

Title: PostgreSQL: Re: Pattern with backslash commands in psql terminal
URL: https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/17253.1148409362%40sss.pgh.pa.us
Published: 2006-05-23T18:36:02.000Z
Author: Tom Lane
Highlights:
No, it's more a shell-style pattern. Use "*" and "?". "." separates schema and object name parts of the pattern.

...

The various \d commands accept a pattern parameter to specify the object name(s) to be displayed. * means "any sequence of characters" and ? means "any single character". (This notation is comparable to Unix shell file name patterns.) Advanced users can also use regular-expression notations such as character classes, for example [0-9] to match "any digit". To make any of these pattern-matching characters be interpreted literally, surround it with double quotes. 

A pattern that contains an (unquoted) dot is interpreted as a schema name pattern followed by an object name pattern. For example, \dt foo*.bar* displays all tables in schemas whose name starts with foo and whose table name starts with bar. If no dot appears, then the pattern matches only objects that are visible in the current schema search path. 

Whenever the pattern parameter is omitted completely, the \d commands display all objects that are visible in the current schema search path. To see all objects in the database, use the pattern *.*.

Title: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: 9.7. Pattern Matching
URL: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-matching.html
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
string SIMILAR TO pattern [ESCAPE escape-character]
string NOT SIMILAR TO pattern [ESCAPE escape-character]

...

The `SIMILAR TO` operator returns true or false depending on whether its pattern matches the given string. It is similar to `LIKE`, except that it interprets the pattern using the SQL standard's definition of a regular expression. SQL regular expressions are a curious cross between `LIKE` notation and common (POSIX) regular expression notation.

Like `LIKE`, the `SIMILAR TO` operator succeeds only if its pattern matches the entire string; this is unlike common regular expression behavior where the pattern can match any part of the string. Also like `LIKE`, `SIMILAR TO` uses `_` and `%` as wildcard characters denoting any single character and any string, respectively (these are comparable to `.` and `.*` in POSIX regular expressions).

In addition to these facilities borrowed from `LIKE`, `SIMILAR TO` supports these pattern-matching metacharacters borrowed from POSIX regular expressions:

- `|` denotes alternation (either of two alternatives).
- `*` denotes repetition of the previous item zero or more times.
- `+` denotes repetition of the previous item one or more times.
- `?` denotes repetition of the previous item zero or one time.
- `{``m``}` denotes repetition of the previous item exactly `m` times.
- `{``m``,}` denotes repetition of the previous item `m` or more times.
- `{``m``,``n``}` denotes repetition of the previous item at least `m` and not more than `n` times.
- Parentheses `()` can be used to group items into a single logical item.
- A bracket expression `[...]` specifies a character class, just as in POSIX regular expressions.

Notice that the period (`.`) is not a metacharacter for `SIMILAR TO`.

As with `LIKE`, a backslash disables the special meaning of any of these metacharacters. A different escape character can be specified with `ESCAPE`, or the escape capability can be disabled by writing `ESCAPE ''`.

...

Some examples:

```
'abc' SIMILAR TO 'abc'          true
'abc' SIMILAR TO 'a'            false
'abc' SIMILAR TO '%(b|d)%'      true
'abc' SIMILAR TO '(b|c)%'       false
'-abc-' SIMILAR TO '%\mabc\M%'  true
'xabcy' SIMILAR TO '%\mabc\M%'  false

```

...

A regular expression is a character sequence that is an abbreviated definition of a set of strings (a regular set). A string is said to match a regular expression if it is a member of the regular set described by the regular expression. As with `LIKE`, pattern characters match string characters exactly unless they are special characters in the regular expression language — but regular expressions use different special characters than `LIKE` does. Unlike `LIKE` patterns, a regular expression is allowed to match anywhere within a string, unless the regular expression is explicitly anchored to the beginning or end of the string.

Some examples:

```
'abcd' ~ 'bc'     true
'abcd' ~ 'a.c'    true — dot matches any character
'abcd' ~ 'a.*d'   true — * repeats the preceding pattern item
'abcd' ~ '(b|x)'  true — | means OR, parentheses group
'abcd' ~ '^a'     true — ^ anchors to start of string
'abcd' ~ '^(b|c)' false — would match except for anchoring

...

A regular expression is defined as one or more branches, separated by `|`. It matches anything that matches one of the branches.

...

Table 9.21. Regular Expression Class-Shorthand Escapes

| Escape | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `\d` | matches any digit, like `[[:digit:]]` |
| `\s` | matches any whitespace character, like `[[:space:]]` |
| `\w` | matches any word character, like `[[:word:]]` |
| `\D` | matches any non-digit, like `[^[:digit:]]` |
| `\S` | matches any non-whitespace character, like `[^[:space:]]` |
| `\W` | matches any non-word character, like `[^[:word:]]` |

The class-shorthand escapes also work within bracket expressions, although the definitions shown above are not quite syntactically valid in that context. For example, `[a-c\d]` is equivalent to `[a-c[:digit:]]`.

Title: Data Types
URL: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongodb-shell/reference/data-types
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
MongoDB stores data using BSON, which supports additional data types that aren't available in JSON. The `mongosh` shell has better data type support for drivers than the legacy `mongo` shell.

...

## Double

The Double() constructor can be used to explicitly specify a double:

```javascript
db.types.insertOne(
   {
      "_id": 2,
      "value": Double(1),
      "expectedType": "Double"
   }
)

```

Note:

If field's value is a number that can be converted to a 32-bit integer, `mongosh` will store it as `Int32`. If not, `mongosh` defaults to storing the number as a `Double`. To specify the value type, use the `Double()` or `Int32()` constructors.

## Int32

The Int32() constructor can be used to explicitly specify 32-bit integers.

```javascript
db.types.insertOne(
   {
       "_id": 1,
       "value": Int32(1),
       "expectedType": "Int32"
   }
)

```

Warning:

Default `Int32` and `Double` types may be stored inconsistently if you connect to the same collection using both `mongosh` and the legacy `mongo` shell.

...

## Type Checking

Use the `$type` query operator or examine the object constructor to determine types.

The Javascript `typeof` operator returns generic values such as `number` or `object` rather than the more specific `Int32` or `ObjectId`.

Javascript's `instanceof` operator is not reliable. For example, `instanceof` assigns BSON values in a server response to a different base class than user supplied values.

For usage examples, see Type Checking with $type() and Type Checking with a Constructor.

...

### Default Numeric Type Consistency

Consider the `typeExample` collection. This collection consists of two identical documents, `{ "a": 1 }`. The first document was created in the legacy `mongo` shell, the second document was created in `mongosh`.

We can use the `$type` operator in an aggregation pipeline to see the type that was assigned in each shell.

```javascript
db.typeExample.aggregate(
  [
    {
       $project:
         {
           "valueType":
             {
               "$type": "$a"
             },
           "_id": 0
         }
    }
  ]
)

```

In the first document, created in the legacy `mongo` shell, the value was stored as a `double`. In the `mongosh` document the value was stored as type `int`.

```javascript
..
[
  {
     valueType: 'double'  // inserted in legacy mongo shell
  },
  {
     valueType: 'int'     // inserted in mongosh
  }
]

```

Show

 Unlike mongo where numbers are always stored as doubles unless differently specified, mongosh will have the javascript behavior: 1 is an int32, 1.1 is a double. 

### Description

mongosh should insert number as Double by default. 

Currently number in mongosh are inserted as int32 if they can be represented as integer and as double otherwise.

ie.

```
db.coll1.insertOne({
  x: 1
});

```

will result in a bson document like this:

```
{
    _id: 602aa63a5eabf03429d733f1,
    x: Int32 { _bsontype: 'Int32', value: 1 }
}

```

where the old shell would have inserted a Double:

```
{
    _id: 602aa5da098e6ce990139172,
    x: Double { _bsontype: 'Double', value: 1 }
}

```

Title: Numbers, Dates, and Decimal128 – The Document Model and BSON – MongoDB | Web Coding Center
URL: https://webcodingcenter.com/mongodb/the-document-model-and-bson--numbers-dates-and-decimal128.html
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
BSON has four numeric types where JavaScript has one, and the driver picks between them for you. An integral JavaScript number within the signed 32-bit range serializes as Int32 (type 16, 4 bytes); every other number — fractional, or beyond ±2^31 — becomes a double (type 1, 8 bytes), exact only to 2^53. Long (type 18, 8 bytes) is the explicit 64-bit integer; a one-field document holding an Int32 measures 12 bytes against 16 for a Double or a Long. Decimal128 (type 19, 16 bytes) is IEEE 754 decimal floating point with 34 significant digits and base-10 arithmetic — the type for money.

Four numeric types, and what each one keeps JavaScript

```javascript
import { serialize, deserialize, Long, Decimal128 } from 'bson';
const back = (d) => deserialize(serialize(d));
const bsonType = (v) => serialize({ v })[4];        // the type byte of the only field
console.log(back({ count: 7, ratio: 7.5, big: Long.fromString('9007199254740993') }));
console.log('type bytes  :', [5, 5.5, 2 ** 31].map(bsonType), '(16 = int32, 1 = double)');
console.log('double math :', 0.1 + 0.2);
console.log('decimal doc :', back({ total: Decimal128.fromString('19.99') }));
console.log('date kept   :', back({ at: new Date('2026-09-22T08:30:00.123456Z') }).at);
```

Output

```
{ count: 7, ratio: 7.5, big: new Long('9007199254740993') }
type bytes  : [ 16, 1, 1 ] (16 = int32, 1 = double)
double math : 0.30000000000000004
decimal doc : { total: new Decimal128('19.99') }
date kept   : 2026-09-22T08:30:00.123Z
```

Two lessons sit in that output. 9007199254740993 survives as a Long but would have become 9007199254740992 as a double. And 0.1 + 0.2 is why Decimal128 round-trips 19.99 exactly where a double named price does not: store currency as Decimal128 or as an integer count of cents.

Type is part of identity, and JavaScript hides which one you chose. { qty: 5 } written from mongosh 403 holds an int32, and so does { qty: 5.0 }, because the two literals are the same number in JavaScript; only Double(5) forces a double. A query for { qty: 5 } matches all of them, but { qty: { $type: 'int' } } matches the first two. Keep a single type per field, and repair a mixed one with $toInt or $toDecimal (The Aggregation Pipeline).

Title: Double and Int32 | mongodb/js-bson | DeepWiki
URL: https://deepwiki.com/mongodb/js-bson/3.5-double-and-int32
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
## Overview Copy link to header

BSON distinguishes between 64-bit IEEE 754 floating-point numbers (BSON type `0x01`, `BSON_DATA_NUMBER`) and 32-bit signed integers (BSON type `0x10`, `BSON_DATA_INT`). The library provides a wrapper class for each:

| Class | BSON type byte | `_bsontype` | Wire size | JS storage |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Double` | `0x01` | `'Double'` | 8 bytes | `number` (float64) |
| `Int32` | `0x10` | `'Int32'` | 4 bytes | `number` (int32) |

Both extend `BSONValue` and implement the same interface pattern: a `.value` property, `valueOf()`, `toJSON()`, `toString()`, `toExtendedJSON()`, `fromExtendedJSON()`, and `inspect()`.

...

### Constructor Copy link to header

```
new Double(value: number)

```

The constructor is defined at src/double.ts 27-34 It accepts a primitive `number`. If a `Number` object (boxed) is passed, it is unwrapped via `.valueOf()`. The stored value is set with the unary `+` operator, which coerces strings at runtime despite the TypeScript signature only listing `number`.

| Input type | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `number` primitive | Stored as-is |
| `Number` object | Unwrapped to primitive |
| string (runtime) | Coerced with unary `+` |

Special values (`Infinity`, `-Infinity`, `NaN`, `-0`) are preserved exactly.

...

### Constructor Copy link to header

```
new Int32(value: number | string)

```

Defined at src/int_32.ts 29-36 The constructor accepts both `number` and `string`. The stored value is computed as `+value | 0`: the unary `+` coerces to a number, and the bitwise OR with `0` truncates to a signed 32-bit integer. This means:

- Values outside the int32 range are silently truncated (wrapping behavior).
- Floating-point values are truncated toward zero.
- `Number` objects are unwrapped before coercion.

Unlike `Double.fromString()`, this constructor does not validate the input string for formatting.

### `Int32.fromString()` Copy link to header

Defined at src/int_32.ts 51-67 This static method enforces strict validation. It uses `removeLeadingZerosAndExplicitPlus` (from `src/utils/string_utils`) to normalize the string before comparison.

Accepted formats:

- Plain decimal integers: `'42'`, `'-5600'`, `'000042'`

...

| Condition | Example |

...

| --- | --- | --- |
| Value > `BSON_INT32_MAX` (2147483647) | `'2147483648'` | `is larger than the maximum value for Int32` |
| Value < `BSON_INT32_MIN` (-2147483648) | `'-2147483649'` | `is smaller than the minimum value for Int32` |
| Not a safe integer | `'2.0'`, `'1.5'` | `is not a safe integer` |
| Non-integer string that coerces differently | `'24,000'`, `'0x1f'`, `'1e2'` | `is not a valid Int32 string` |

...

Defined at src/int_32.ts 93-95 Parses the `$numberInt` string:

- Relaxed: `parseInt(doc.$numberInt, 10)` — plain JS number

...

## Serialization and Deserialization Copy link to header

How the serializer selects the BSON type byte

The serializer in `src/parser/serializer.ts` dispatches on `_bsontype`. A plain JavaScript number is serialized as either `BSON_DATA_INT` (`0x10`) if it fits in 32 bits, or `BSON_DATA_NUMBER` (`0x01`) otherwise. Wrapping a value explicitly in `Double` or `Int32` forces the corresponding wire type regardless of value magnitude.

| Type | Constant | Bytes | Encoding |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Double` | `BSON_DATA_NUMBER = 0x01` | 8 | IEEE 754 double, little-endian |
| `Int32` | `BSON_DATA_INT = 0x10` | 4 | Signed 32-bit integer, little-endian |

Special `Double` values (`-0`, `NaN` with payload, `Infinity`) round-trip exactly through BSON serialization test/node/double.test.ts 299-333

### Effect of `promoteValues` on Deserialized Output Copy link to header

The `promoteValues` deserialization option controls whether wrapper objects or plain primitives are returned. The default is `true`.

| `promoteValues` | BSON type `0x01` result | BSON type `0x10` result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `true` (default) | plain `number` | plain `number` |
| `false` | `Double` instance | `Int32` instance |

When `promoteValues: false`, the returned objects have `_bsontype === 'Double'` or `_bsontype === 'Int32'` and their `.value` holds the parsed number.

Title: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: 32.16. The Password File
URL: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/libpq-pgpass.html
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
The file `.pgpass` in a user's home directory can contain passwords to be used if the connection requires a password (and no password has been specified otherwise). On Unix systems, the directory can be specified by the `HOME` environment variable, or if undefined, the home directory of the effective user. On Microsoft Windows the file is named `%APPDATA%\postgresql\pgpass.conf` (where `%APPDATA%` refers to the Application Data subdirectory in the user's profile). Alternatively, the password file to use can be specified using the connection parameter passfile or the environment variable `PGPASSFILE`.

This file should contain lines of the following format:

```
hostname:port:database:username:password

```

(You can add a reminder comment to the file by copying the line above and preceding it with `#`.) Each of the first four fields can be a literal value, or `*`, which matches anything. The password field from the first line that matches the current connection parameters will be used. (Therefore, put more-specific entries first when you are using wildcards.) If an entry needs to contain `:` or `\`, escape this character with `\`. The host name field is matched to the `host` connection parameter if that is specified, otherwise to the `hostaddr` parameter if that is specified; if neither are given then the host name `localhost` is searched for. The host name `localhost` is also searched for when the connection is a Unix-domain socket connection and the `host` parameter matches libpq's default socket directory path. In a standby server, a database field of `replication` matches streaming replication connections made to the primary server. The database field is of limited usefulness otherwise, because users have the same password for all databases in the same cluster.

Title: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: 32.1. Database Connection Control Functions
URL: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/libpq-connect.html
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
Without either a host name or host address, libpq will connect using a local Unix-domain socket; or on Windows, it will attempt to connect to `localhost`.
`port`#
: Port number to connect to at the server host, or socket file name extension for Unix-domain connections. If multiple hosts were given in the `host` or `hostaddr` parameters, this parameter may specify a comma-separated list of ports of the same length as the host list, or it may specify a single port number to be used for all hosts. An empty string, or an empty item in a comma-separated list, specifies the default port number established when PostgreSQL was built.
`dbname`#
: The database name. Defaults to be the same as the user name. In certain contexts, the value is checked for extended formats; see Section 32.1.1 for more details on those.
`user`#
: PostgreSQL user name to connect as. Defaults to be the same as the operating system name of the user running the application.
`password`#
: Password to be used if the server demands password authentication.
`passfile`#
: Specifies the name of the file used to store passwords (see Section 32.16). Defaults to `~/.pgpass`, or `%APPDATA%\postgresql\pgpass.conf` on Microsoft Windows. (No error is reported if this file does not exist.)
`require_auth`#
: Specifies the authentication method that the client requires from the server. If the server does not use the required method to authenticate the client, or if the authentication handshake is not fully completed by the server, the connection will fail. A comma-separated list of methods may also be provided, of which the server must use exactly one in order for the connection to succeed. By default, any authentication method is accepted, and the server is free to skip authentication altogether.
